questions.prompt: Decide whether W = {p in \(P_2\) : \(p(0)\) = 0} is a subspace of \(P_2\).
questions.answer: The zero polynomial satisfies \(p(0)\) = 0, so it is in W. If p and q are in W, then (p + q)(0) = \(p(0)\) + q(0) = 0 + 0 = 0, so p + q is in W. If c is real and p is in W, then (cp)(0) = c \(p(0)\) = \(c\cdot0\) = 0, so cp is in W. Therefore W is a subspace of \(P_2\).

questions.prompt: Decide whether W = {p in \(P_2\) : \(p(0)\) = 1} is a subspace of \(P_2\).
questions.answer: The zero polynomial has value 0 at \(x=0\), not 1. Therefore the zero vector of \(P_2\) is not in W. Since every subspace must contain the zero vector, W is not a subspace of \(P_2\).

questions.prompt: Decide whether the set of \(2\times 2\) matrices with trace 0 is a subspace of \(M_{2,2}(\mathbb R)\).
questions.answer: The zero matrix has trace 0, so it is in the set. If A and B have trace 0, then \(\operatorname{tr}(A + B)\) = \(\operatorname{tr}(A)\) + \(\operatorname{tr}(B)\) = 0. If c is real, then \(\operatorname{tr}(cA)\) = c \(\operatorname{tr}(A)\) = 0. Therefore the set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so it is a subspace.

questions.prompt: Decide whether the set of \(2\times 2\) matrices with determinant 0 is a subspace of \(M_{2,2}(\mathbb R)\).
questions.answer: It is not a subspace because addition closure fails. Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Both have determinant 0. But A + \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), which has determinant 1. Therefore A + B is not in the set, so the set is not a subspace.

questions.prompt: Decide whether the set of even functions is a subspace of the vector space of all real-valued functions on \(\mathbb R\).
questions.answer: The zero function is even because 0(-x) = 0 = 0(x). If f and g are even, then (f + g)(-x) = f(-x) + g(-x) = f(x) + g(x) = (f + g)(x), so f + g is even. If c is real, then (cf)(-x) = c f(-x) = c f(x) = (cf)(x), so cf is even. Therefore the even functions form a subspace.

questions.prompt: Decide whether the set of functions f with \(f(1)\) >= 0 is a subspace of all real-valued functions on \(\mathbb R\).
questions.answer: Scalar closure fails. For example, the constant function f(x) = 1 satisfies \(f(1)\) = 1 >= 0, so it is in the set. But (-1)f has value -1 at \(x=1\), which is not >= 0. Therefore the set is not a subspace.

questions.prompt: Show that the set of polynomials in \(P_3\) with zero \(x^2\) coefficient is a subspace of \(P_3\).
questions.answer: The zero polynomial has \(x^2\) coefficient 0. If p and q both have \(x^2\) coefficient 0, then p + q has \(x^2\) coefficient 0 + 0 = 0. If c is real and p has \(x^2\) coefficient 0, then cp has \(x^2\) coefficient \(c\cdot0\) = 0. Therefore the set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so it is a subspace.

questions.prompt: Decide whether the set of upper triangular \(2\times 2\) matrices is a subspace of \(M_{2,2}(\mathbb R)\).
questions.answer: An upper triangular \(2\times 2\) matrix has the form \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{pmatrix}\). The zero matrix has this form. The sum of \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}e&f\\0&g\end{pmatrix}\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}a + e&b + f\\0&d + g\end{pmatrix}\), also upper triangular. A scalar multiple c\(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}ca&cb\\0&cd\end{pmatrix}\) is also upper triangular. Therefore the set is a subspace.

questions.prompt: Decide whether the set of invertible \(2\times 2\) matrices is a subspace of \(M_{2,2}(\mathbb R)\).
questions.answer: It is not a subspace. A subspace must contain the zero vector, but the zero matrix is not invertible. Also, scalar closure fails because multiplying an invertible matrix by 0 gives the zero matrix, which is not invertible. Therefore the invertible \(2\times 2\) matrices do not form a subspace.

questions.prompt: A learner says every subset closed under addition is a subspace. Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: A subspace must also be closed under scalar multiplication and contain the zero vector. Closure under addition alone is not enough. For example, the positive real numbers are closed under addition, but multiplying a positive number by -1 gives a negative number, so scalar closure fails. Therefore addition closure alone does not prove a subspace.
